content: Giardiasis is an intestinal infection caused by the protozoan parasite Giardia lamblia. This parasite is flagellated and is transmitted primarily through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated water, food, or direct contact with infected individuals. It is a global health concern, particularly in areas with poor sanitation. The infection can be classified as acute, lasting 2 to 4 weeks, or chronic, persisting for more than 4 weeks. Other risk factors include immunosuppression, young age (especially children under 5 years old), contact with infected individuals, consumption of unsafe water, unprotected anal or oral-anal sexual contact, and recent travel to developing countries. After transmission, the parasite colonizes the human intestine, attaching to the epithelial lining via a ventral adhesive disc. The resulting immune response, particularly involving CD8+ T-cells, causes local inflammation and damage to the microvilli, impairing nutrient absorption and exacerbating symptoms. The clinical presentation of giardiasis varies. In the acute phase, symptoms typically include profuse watery diarrhea, bloating, abdominal cramping, and flatulence. These symptoms are often self-limiting. However, in some cases, the infection progresses to a chronic phase, characterized by persistent diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss, malaise, and failure to thrive. Rare complications include severe dehydration, malabsorption (e.g., vitamin B12 deficiency), post-infectious syndromes such as reactive arthritis or chronic fatigue syndrome, and, in rare cases, dissemination of the parasite to extraluminal sites like the gallbladder, pancreas, or eyes. The diagnosis of giardiasis is confirmed by detecting Giardia cysts or trophozoites in stool samples. Since the excretion of cysts is intermittent, it is recommended to collect and examine at least three stool samples on separate days to improve diagnostic sensitivity. Fecal immunoassays and molecular techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), may also be employed, particularly when stool microscopy is inconclusive. Additional diagnostic methods, such as the string test or small bowel biopsy, may be considered in cases of diagnostic uncertainty or persistent symptoms despite treatment. Treatment of giardiasis involves antimicrobial therapy. First-line medications include metronidazole, albendazole, or quinacrine. In pediatric patients, furazolidone or nitazoxanide may be used. Patients should be monitored for symptom resolution, as persistent or recurrent symptoms may indicate treatment failure or reinfection. Preventive strategies focus on improving hygiene practices, such as regular handwashing and ensuring access to safe drinking water, to reduce the risk of transmission. The prognosis for giardiasis is generally excellent, although recurrence is common, particularly in children, even with appropriate treatment.
